en: Majjhima Nikāya 51,
the Kandarakasutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then Pessa, the son of a charioteer, and the wanderer Kandaka approached the Blessed One. Having approached, Pessa, the son of a charioteer, paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
But the wanderer Kandaka exchanged greetings with the Blessed One; when they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the wanderer Kandaraka surveyed the silent community of monks and said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
To what an extent the community of monks has been properly guided by Master Gotama!”
"Those who were the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, in the past, O Gotama, those Blessed Ones also guided the community of monks rightly to this very extent—
as the community of monks is now being guided rightly by Master Gotama.
And those who will be the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, in the future, O Gotama, those Blessed Ones also will guide the community of monks rightly to this very extent."
“Just as the Blessed One Gotama now rightly leads the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
“It is so, Kandaraka; it is so, Kandaraka.
Those who were the Arahants, the Fully Enlightened Ones, in the past, those Blessed Ones also led the Saṅgha of bhikkhus rightly to this very extent.”
Just as the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is now rightly led by me,
so too, Kandaraka, those who will be Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones in future time, those Blessed Ones will lead the Saṅgha of bhikkhus rightly to this very same extent—
just as the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is now rightly led by me.

For there are, Kandaraka, monks in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are completely liberated through final knowledge.
For there are, Kandaraka, monks in this Saṅgha of bhikkhus who are trainees, consistent in virtue, consistent in conduct, prudent, and prudent in conduct;
they dwell with minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness.
In which four?
Here, Kandaraka, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
When this was said, Pessa, the son of a charioteer, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!

How well these four foundations of mindfulness have been expounded by the Blessed One for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of nibbāna.”
for the realization of Nibbāna.
For we too, venerable sir, being white-robed laypeople, dwell from time to time with our minds well-established in these four foundations of mindfulness.
Here, venerable sir, we dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
We dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
we dwell contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
we dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir!
To such an extent, venerable sir, does the Blessed One know the welfare and harm of beings while humanity is thus dense, thus deceitful, and thus treacherous.
For this, venerable sir, is a density: namely, human beings.
"Venerable sir, this matter regarding cattle is indeed superficial. For I, venerable sir,

am capable of training a tame elephant so that it will travel back and forth between Campa in whatever time it takes, and it will display all its tricks, deceits, crookednesses, and devious maneuvers."
"But for us, Bhante, whether they are called slaves, messengers, or laborers, they behave toward us with one kind of body, another kind of speech, and their minds are yet another.
It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante!
To such an extent, Bhante, does the Blessed One know the welfare and harm of beings while such human density, such human deceit, and such human guile are prevailing."
“Venerable sir, this human condition is indeed deep;
this condition of animals, venerable sir, is shallow.
“It is so, Pessa; it is so, Pessa.”
This world of humans, Pessa, is indeed dense;
this world of cattle, Pessa, is indeed shallow.
There are these four types of persons, Pessa, found existing in the world.
Which four?
Here, Pessa, one person torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment;
here, Pessa, another person torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
But here, Pessa, a certain person torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and he also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
But here, Pessa, a certain person neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
Not tormenting himself and not tormenting others, he dwells in this very life free from craving, extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, having become one with the Brahma-nature.
“Of these four persons, Pessa, which one wins your heart?
“Venerable sir, that person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment does not win my heart.
That person who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others—this person also does not win my heart.”
"Venerable sir, that person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others—
this person does not satisfy my mind. But as for this other person, venerable sir, who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment,
and who neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others— he, not tormenting himself and not tormenting others, is free from hunger in this very life."
“Extinguished, cooled, experiencing bliss, he dwells having become Brahmā himself—
this person alone wins my heart.
“But why, Pessa, do these three persons not win your heart?”
“Bhante, when this person who torments himself is devoted to the practice of self-torment, he torments and afflicts himself— who desires happiness and recoils from suffering—
it is for this reason that this person does not satisfy my mind. Bhante,
when this person who torments others is devoted to the practice of tormenting others, he torments and afflicts another— who desires happiness and recoils from suffering— ”
"Because of this, this person does not please my mind.

Furthermore, venerable sir, that person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others— tormenting and tormenting both himself and others who desire happiness and recoil from suffering—
because of this, this person does not please my mind."
But as for this person, venerable sir, who neither torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment,
and neither torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others— he, not tormenting himself and not tormenting others, being free from hunger even in this very life,
extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, dwells with a self that has become sublime.
Since he neither torments nor causes others to torment himself or another who both desires happiness and recoils from suffering—
by this means this person wins my heart.
Now, venerable sir, we shall depart.
“We have many duties; we have much to do.
“Then, Pessa, go at whatever time you deem appropriate.

Then Pessa, the son of a charioteer, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, not long after Pessa Hatthārohaputta had departed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, Pessa Hatthārohaputta is wise;
bhikkhus, Pessa Hatthārohaputta possesses great wisdom."
“Bhikkhus, if Pessa, the son of a charioteer, were to sit for a moment while I analyze these four persons in detail, he would be endowed with great benefit.
Yet, bhikkhus, even to this extent, Pessa, the son of a charioteer, is already endowed with great benefit.
“This is the time for that, Blessed One; this is the time for that, Sugata.”
“May the Blessed One analyze these four types of persons in detail. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.
“In that case, monks, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, monks, is the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment?

Here, monks, a certain person goes naked, rejecting conventions, licking his hands, not coming when asked, not staying when asked; he does not accept food brought to him, nor food prepared for him, nor an invitation.”
He does not accept food brought to him, nor food specially prepared for him, nor an invitation;
he does not receive it from the mouth of a storage jar, nor from the mouth of a basket, nor across a sheepskin, nor across a staff, nor across a pestle;
he does not accept food from two people eating together, nor from a pregnant woman, nor from a woman nursing, nor from a woman in the presence of her husband.
He does not frequent villages, nor where that [food] is available, nor where flies swarm in clusters;
he drinks no fish, no meat, no wine, no liquor, and no grain-beer.

He becomes one who goes for alms at a single house, or eats a single morsel; or he becomes one who goes for alms at two houses, or eats two morsels …pe… or he becomes one who goes for alms at seven houses, or eats seven morsels.
He subsists on a single alms-meal, or he subsists on two alms-meals …pe… or he subsists on seven alms-meals;

he takes food once a day, or he takes food once every two days …pe… or he takes food once every seven days—in this way, he dwells devoted to the practice of taking meals at regular intervals for up to half a month.
He becomes one who eats greens, or one who eats millet, or one who eats wild rice, or one who eats horse-gram.
He eats only once a day, or he eats every second day, or he eats every third day, or he eats every fourth day, or he eats every seventh day;

he subsists on a single handful of rice per day, or he eats only broken rice, or he eats only husked rice, or he eats only the scum of boiled rice, or he eats only oil-cake, or he eats only grass, or he eats only cow dung; he sustains himself by feeding on forest roots and fruits, eating only what has fallen of its own accord.
He wears robes of hemp, or robes of hemp-mixed cloth, or shrouds from corpses, or rag-robes from dust heaps.
He wears garments made of tirīṭa grass; he wears deerskins; he wears strips of deerskin; he wears garments of kusa grass; he wears garments of bark;
he wears garments of wood-shavings; he wears a blanket of human hair; he wears a blanket of animal fur;
he wears a cloak of owl feathers.
He is one who plucks out his hair and beard, devoted to the practice of plucking out his hair and beard;
he is one who stands continuously, rejecting seats;
he is one who squats, devoted to the exertion of squatting.
He is one who uses a bed of thorns, spreading his bed upon a bed of thorns;
he dwells devoted to the practice of descending into water for a third time every night—
thus he dwells devoted to various kinds of such practices involving the mortification and tormenting of the body.
“Monks, this is called the person who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of torturing himself.
And what, monks, is the person who torments others and is devoted to the practice of torturing others?

Here, monks, a certain person is a butcher of sheep, a butcher of pigs, a fowler, a hunter, a trapper, a fisherman, a thief, an executioner, a butcher of cattle, a jailer, or anyone else engaged in cruel occupations.”
“Monks, this person is called one who torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
And what, monks, is the person who both torments himself and is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, and also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others?
Here, monks, a certain person is either a head-anointed kshatriya king or a wealthy brahmin.”
Thus, having had a new assembly hall built to the east of the city, having shaved off his hair and beard, having put on a rough antelope skin,
and having anointed his body with ghee and oil, he entered the new assembly hall together with his chief queen and the brahmin family priest, scratching his back with a deer horn.
Thus, there he makes his bed upon the bare ground smeared with green cow dung.
A certain cow with a calf of similar appearance has milk in one udder with which the king subsists;
the milk in the second udder with which the chief queen subsists; the milk in the third udder...
With that [milk], the brahmin family priest is sustained; with the milk that remains from the fourth portion, he offers oblations to the fire;
and with what is left over, the calf is sustained.
He spoke thus:
‘Let so many bulls be slain for the sake of sacrifice; let so many bullocks be slain for the sake of sacrifice;
let so many heifers be slain for the sake of sacrifice; let so many goats be slain for the sake of sacrifice; let so many rams be slain for the sake of sacrifice;
let so many horses be slain for the sake of sacrifice; let so many trees be cut down for the sake of sacrificial posts.’
"Let this much grass be cut for the purpose of making a sacrificial bed.
And those who are his slaves, messengers, or laborers—they too perform their tasks driven by the threat of punishment and the fear of danger, weeping with tearful faces.
This person, monks, is called one who torments himself and is devoted to the practice of self-torment, and who also torments others and is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
And what kind of person, monks, is neither one who torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of self-torment,
nor one who torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others; who, neither tormenting himself nor tormenting others,
is in this very life free from craving, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, and dwells with a self that has become sublime?

"Here, monks, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known."
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Endowed with that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
"Household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is the open air.
It is not easy for one living at home to lead the holy life in its full perfection, purity, and polished completeness."
‘What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or large mass of wealth,
and having abandoned a small or large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard.
Having clothed himself in saffron robes, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having thus gone forth, endowed with the training and the livelihood of the bhikkhus, he abandons the taking of life and abstains from taking life;
having laid aside the rod and laid aside the weapon, he dwells conscientious, compassionate, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart pure and free from theft.
Having abandoned unchastity, he lives a life of chastity; he dwells aloof, refraining from sexual intercourse, the common practice of the village.
Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he is a speaker of truth, devoted to truth, trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech.

Having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people; nor, having heard something there, does he repeat it to these people for the purpose of dividing those people.

Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united. Delighting in concord, rejoicing in concord, finding joy in concord, he speaks words that create concord.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; he speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-touching, urbane, agreeable to many people, and beloved by many people.

Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks on the Dhamma, speaks on the Vinaya; he speaks at the proper time words that are worth treasuring, accompanied by reasons, measured, and beneficial.
He abstains from damaging seeds and plants.
He eats but one meal a day, refrains from eating at night, and abstains from eating at improper times;
he abstains from dancing, singing, instrumental music, and witnessing shows;
he abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes and scents, and from the use of cosmetics and ornaments for beautification.
He abstains from high and luxurious beds and seats;
he abstains from accepting gold and silver;
he abstains from accepting raw grain.
He abstains from accepting raw meat;
he abstains from accepting women and girls;
he abstains from accepting male and female slaves.
He abstains from accepting goats and sheep;
he abstains from accepting chickens and pigs;
he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares.
He abstains from accepting fields and land;
he abstains from engaging in the business of running errands and acting as a messenger;
he abstains from buying and selling.
He abstains from cheating with scales, cheating with measures, and cheating with weights;
he abstains from bribery, deception, and fraud;
he abstains from mutilation, execution, imprisonment, robbery, plunder, and violence.
Thus he is content with robes that serve to protect the body and with almsfood that serves to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking these with him.

Just as a winged bird, wherever it flies, flies carrying its wings, even so a bhikkhu is content with robes that serve to protect the body and with almsfood that serves to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking these with him.
Thus, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the happiness of blamelessness.
Having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
For if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.

If, when he has seen a form with the eye, there should arise in him such mental states that would flow in upon him, he practices for their restraint; he guards the faculty of the eye, he attains restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
[and so on] ...having smelled an odor with the nose... [and so on] ...
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having touched a tangible object with the body … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind,
he does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
If, when one dwells with this faculty of mind unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—should flow in after him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of mind and attains restraint over the faculty of mind.
Possessed of this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself the unsullied happiness.
Thus, he acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when defecating and urinating.
Whether going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, or remaining silent,
he acts with clear comprehension. Thus, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble contentment,
endowed with this noble restraint of the sense faculties, and endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension...
He frequents a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Having returned from his almsround after his meal, he sits down, crosses his legs, sets his body erect, and establishes mindfulness before him.
Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings, and purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending, and purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly tranquil, and purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—he, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

With the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses rapture and happiness born of concentration.
And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: "He dwells happily, mindful and equanimous"—thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind to the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births... [and so on].
Whether four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births,
a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, or many aeons of world-contraction,
many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion: "In that place I was..."
‘I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose there; and there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I was reborn here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their modes and details.
He recollects his past lives.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs it toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn.
He understands beings as they pass away and reappear—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—according to their kamma:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, possessed of misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views. With the breakup of the body..."
...after the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell; whereas these worthy beings,
having been endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, endowed with good conduct of mind,
not reviling the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view— these, after the breakup of the body, after death...

‘Having died, they have been reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.

With his mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
Thus he understands as it really is: “This is suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”; he understands as it really is:
“This is the cessation of suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
‘These are the taints,’ he understands as it really is. ‘This is the origin of the taints,’ he understands as it really is.
‘This is the cessation of the taints,’ he understands as it really is. ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints,’ he understands as it really is.

For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no further state of being in this world."

“Monks, this person is said to be neither one who torments himself nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting himself, nor one who torments others nor is devoted to the practice of tormenting others.
Tormenting neither himself nor others, he dwells in this very life free from hunger, extinguished, become cool, experiencing happiness, with his self become as Brahmā.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The Kandarakasutta, the first, is finished.
